newsitem.title: GERMANY: German experts slam plan to revalue reserves.
newsitem.headline: German experts slam plan to revalue reserves.

text.p: German economic experts warned the government Friday that a plan to revalue central bank reserves could jeopardise European monetary union and said it might not solve Bonn's budgetary impasse.

But Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt defended the plan, hammered out in an agreement between Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer on Thursday as a legitimate way of boosting revenue.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats, argued that the plan, which could provide Bonn with well over 10 billion marks ($5.8 billion) in additional revenue, was not to fill budget gaps but to erase debt inherited from former communist East Germany.
Heiner Flassbeck, chief economist at the Berlin-based German Institute for Economic Research, said Bonn was conducting "a currency and economic policy bordering on the limits of respectability."
This could have dire consequences not only for Germany but for the rest of Europe in its drive for economic and monetary union, Flassbeck told the Neue Osnabruecker Zeitung daily.
"The whole thing is accompanied by a deflation policy, which will drag the whole of Europe into the same pot and undermine the foundations for European monetary union."

Flassbeck said there was no guarantee the European Union would recognise windfall profits from revaluation as a way of reducing the budget deficit when it chooses which countries qualify for EMU since this breached the principle of sustainability enshrined in the Maastricht Treaty.

Rolf Peffekoven, one of the "Five Wise Men" advising the government on economic policy, said that the move should not be overrated and that there was little chance it would improve Bonn's financial crisis.
"We need lasting and solid finances and this has not been achieved through this. The main problem in Germany remains the high budget deficit," Peffekoven told ZDF television.
He said that even if profits created by the revaluation reduced debt and improved public deficit figures, these would not be greatly improved.

Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier, finance expert for the opposition SPD, told MDR radio that the plan amounted to printing new banknotes, which would not stop budget gaps but only perpetuate Bonn's "budget chaos."

"Profits on paper are to be transferred to the market -- this is just creating money. No problems are solved by it. In 1997 we will be short of 15 billion marks, in 1998 -- 32 billion marks. The (financial) chaos just goes on," she said.

Rexrodt hit back at his critics, saying in an interview with German radio that the plan was "inevitable and legitimate." FDP economic expert Paul Friedhoff said it was "not to stop budget gaps but to retire debt."

The deal reflects a compromise allowing Bonn to benefit from the revaluation of foreign exchange reserves but leaves central bank gold reserves untouched until after the scheduled launch of EMU in 1999.

The Bundesbank on Thursday dismissed statements by sources in the Bonn coalition government who said Waigel and Tietmeyer agreed the central bank would revalue dollar reserves at a rate of at least 1.50 marks per dollar. The dollar currently trades above 1.70 marks on the foreign exchange market.

The Bundesbank's currency reserves of $65.7 billion are thought to consist only of dollars and are currently booked at 1.3620 marks. Bonn coalition sources said this meant the central bank could transfer as much as 13 billion marks to the government next year as part of the deal.
